races.long_description: Representative Barry Moore, a third-term Republican and longtime Trump loyalist, is running for the Senate seat being vacated by Tommy Tuberville, who is running for governor. Mr. Moore’s Democratic opponent, Everett Wess, a former judge and lawyer, is a long shot in deep-red Alabama.

Senator Dan S. Sullivan, a Republican, is trying to hold on to his seat against former Representative Mary Peltola, a Democrat. The wild card in the four-person ranked-choice race is the presence of Daniel J. Sullivan, a retiree in a small fishing village who has the same name as the incumbent.
Senator Tom Cotton, a Trump ally and the third-ranking Republican in the chamber, is heavily favored to win a third term. He is facing Hallie Shoffner, a Democrat and sixth-generation farmer.

Senator John Hickenlooper, a moderate incumbent, is running for a second term in a solidly Democratic seat. He faces Mark Baisley, a Republican state senator, and Bob Chew, a Navy veteran and former Republican who is running as an independent.

Senator Chris Coons, a Democrat, is heavily favored to win re-election in a state that Kamala Harris carried by about 15 percentage points two years ago. His Republican challenger is Mike Katz, a doctor who has served in Delaware’s State Senate.

Senator Ashley Moody, the Republican incumbent, is on the Senate ballot for the first time, having been appointed last year to finish Marco Rubio’s term. She faces State Representative Angie Nixon, a progressive who won the Democratic primary in an upset.

Senator Jon Ossoff, a Democrat, is seeking a second term in Georgia, a battleground that both parties this cycle initially considered the toughest for Democrats to hold onto. He is facing Representative Mike Collins, a Republican who won President Trump’s endorsement in the primary.

Senator Jim Risch, 83, a Republican, is heavily favored to win a fourth term in Idaho, a state President Trump carried by more than 36 percentage points in 2024. His toughest challenge comes from Todd Achilles, one of several independents challenging Republicans across the country this year.

Illinois’ open Senate seat, now held by retiring Senator Dick Durbin, a Democrat, is likely to remain blue. Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton, a progressive, is favored to prevail over her Republican opponent, Don Tracy, a former chairman of the state Republican Party.

Representative Ashley Hinson, a Republican, is vying to maintain party control of the seat held by retiring Senator Joni Ernst. Polls have shown her locked in a tight race against Josh Turek, a Democratic state representative, in a state that President Trump won three times.

Senator Roger Marshall, a first-term Republican, is trying to survive an unexpectedly competitive race in deep-red Kansas. He faces Adam Hamilton, a centrist Democrat who has sought to corral farmers’ anger at economic conditions under President Trump.

Representative Andy Barr, a Republican, is running to succeed the retiring Senator Mitch McConnell, whose poor health came under scrutiny in recent months. Mr. Barr faces Charles Booker, a progressive former state lawmaker who has run for the Senate twice before.

Senator Bill Cassidy lost his Republican primary this year after President Trump targeted him for voting to convict him in his second impeachment trial. Now the seat Mr. Cassidy held for over a decade is up for grabs, and Representative Julia Letlow, who is backed by Mr. Trump, is heavily favored to win it over Jamie Davis, a Democratic farmer.
Senator Susan Collins, a Republican, is seeking a sixth term against the Democrat Troy Jackson in the toughest political environment she has faced over her 30-year career.

Senator Ed Markey, 80, a Democrat whose progressive bona fides helped him turn back a much younger challenger in the primary, is running for re-election in a solidly Democratic state. He faces John Deaton, a Republican lawyer and a Marine veteran.

Abdul El-Sayed, a Democratic former public health official, is in a competitive race against former Representative Mike Rogers, a Republican who narrowly lost his Senate bid in 2024. The contest has become a key test for progressives, who are backing El-Sayed.

The race to replace the retiring Senator Tina Smith, a Democrat, pits the state’s lieutenant governor, Peggy Flanagan, a Democrat, against Michele Tafoya, a sports journalist and a first-time candidate. The two have sparred over fraud in statewide programs and rising costs attributed to the Iran war and the Trump administration’s tariff policies.

Scott Colom, a Democratic prosecutor, has mounted an unexpectedly competitive challenge to Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, a first-term Republican who has been reliably aligned with President Trump. While Ms. Hyde-Smith is still favored in conservative Mississippi, Mr. Colom would be the first Black senator elected from the state since Reconstruction.

A late withdrawal by the incumbent Republican, Steve Daines, left a Senate seat open in a historically conservative state. Kurt Alme, a Republican backed by President Trump, faces an unusually fractured field after national Democrats and state leaders shifted support toward an independent candidate, Seth Bodnar, instead of the Democrat who won the party’s primary, Alani Bankhead.

Dan Osborn, a mechanic, former union leader and military veteran running as an independent, is challenging Senator Pete Ricketts, a Republican scion of an influential billionaire family with deep ties to Nebraska. To clear the way for Mr. Osborn’s bid, the Democratic primary winner, Cindy Burbank, declined the party’s nomination, potentially consolidating the anti-incumbent vote in the conservative stronghold.

Nearly 20 years ago, John E. Sununu, a Republican, lost his Senate seat to Jeanne Shaheen, a Democrat. Now she is retiring, and Mr. Sununu is trying to make a comeback. He is facing Representative Chris Pappas, a low-key Democrat in his fourth term.
Senator Cory Booker, a Democrat and former Newark mayor elected to the Senate in 2013, faces Justin Murphy, a Republican attorney.

Senator Ben Ray Luján, a Democrat, is running for a second term in a solidly blue state against Larry E. Marker, a former oil and gas producer who won the Republican nomination as a write-in candidate.

Roy Cooper, the Democratic former North Carolina governor, and Michael Whatley, the former Republican National Committee chairman, are competing to succeed Senator Thom Tillis, a Republican who is retiring.

In one of the most expensive and consequential Senate races of this cycle, Senator Jon Husted, a Republican, is facing a challenge from Sherrod Brown, a Democrat. Mr. Brown lost his seat in 2024 after three terms in the Senate.

Markwayne Mullin left the Senate to become secretary of the Department of Homeland Security, and his replacement, Alan Armstrong, is ineligible to seek a full term under state law. Representative Kevin Hern, a Trump ally, is the clear favorite to win the open seat.
Senator Jeff Merkley is running for re-election in a solidly Democratic state. Among his challengers are State Senator David Brock Smith, a Republican, and Gary Lyndon Dye, a Libertarian.

Senator Jack Reed, a Democrat, is seeking a sixth term in a state that has not sent a Republican to the Senate since 2000. He is being challenged by Raymond McKay, a Republican activist who was formerly the network and telecommunications manager for the city of Warwick, R.I.

Senator Darline Graham, the Republican appointed to fill her deceased brother Lindsey Graham’s seat, is running for a full term of her own. Dr. Annie Andrews, a Democrat and a pediatrician, is hoping Ms. Graham’s inexperience and her ties to President Trump can help her flip a seat in a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1998.

Senator Mike Rounds, a Republican, is running for a third term in one of the country’s most conservative states. Public polling has been limited, but some surveys have shown him in a closer-than-usual race with Brian Bengs, an independent. The Democratic nominee withdrew from the ballot.

Senator Bill Hagerty, a Trump-backed Republican, is seeking a second term in a state that President Trump won by nearly 30 points in 2024. His opponent, the Democratic environmental justice activist Marquita Bradshaw, previously ran for Senate in 2020 and 2024.

James Talarico, a state legislator, is trying to become the first Democrat in more than three decades to win a statewide election in Texas. He is facing Ken Paxton, the Republican state attorney general, in a race that is one of the most expensive American campaigns ever.
Senator Mark Warner, a Democrat, is seeking a fourth term in a state that is considered solidly blue. He faces Bert Mizusawa, a retired general who easily won the Republican primary.
Senator Shelley Moore Capito is running for a third term in West Virginia, a Republican stronghold. She faces Rachel Fetty Anderson, a lawyer and a Democratic former city councilwoman in Morgantown.

In deep-red Wyoming, the state’s lone at-large House member, Harriet Hageman, is favored to succeed Senator Cynthia Lummis, a Republican, who is retiring after serving one term. Ms. Hageman faces James Byrd, a Democratic former state lawmaker.

Most voters tend to vote early in person, and vote reporting is usually relatively fast. But if a race is very close, it can still take awhile to declare a winner. In 2022, it took until Wednesday afternoon for The A.P. to declare that the top Senate candidates had advanced to a runoff, which was held on Dec. 6.
In 2022 and 2024, about half of the state’s votes were reported by midnight Eastern time on election night, and the count reached 95 percent around 6 a.m. on Wednesday.

content.text: Peggy Flanagan, the Democratic nominee in Minnesota, is trailing in the Senate race against Michele Tafoya, but a vast majority of the votes in that state have yet to be reported, including in Hennepin and Ramsey counties in the Minneapolis-St. Paul metro area. Two of the largest in the state, these counties are expected to be very favorable for Flanagan.

President Trump won Iowa by 13 percentage points in 2024, but the Senate race there is a microcosm of Republicans’ rough night. Josh Turek, the Democrat, is getting just the kinds of shifts he needs across nearly the entirety of the state. That’s true in urban Democratic-leaning strongholds like Polk County, home to Des Moines, as well as rural Obama-Trump counties like Cerro Gordo.

Darline Graham, who was appointed to the Senate after the death of her brother, Lindsey, in July, said in her concession speech that it had been a difficult few months on the campaign trail. “I would trade this all a thousand times over to have my brother back, but God had a different plan,” she said. She thanked President Trump for his support in the race. “He loves this country dearly,” he said.

Representative Vicente Gonzalez, a Democrat, defeated Eric Flores, a Republican, in Texas’ 34th Congressional District, according to The Associated Press, a victory that suggests Latino voters in the region who had swung Republican in recent elections were frustrated over the cost of living and the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement.

Flores, a former federal prosecutor and Army veteran backed by President Trump, repeatedly attacked Gonzalez as ineffective in Washington while Gonzalez, in turn, portrayed Flores as being in lockstep with the president.

Senator John Cornyn, the Texas Republican who lost his re-election bid after President Trump backed Ken Paxton in the primary, congratulated James Talarico, the Democratic candidate, in a social media post. Though The Times has not yet called the race for Talarico, who is leading in the vote count, Cornyn said that he looked “forward to meeting him and offering my assistance with his transition as he prepares to serve Texans in the U.S. Senate.”

Voters in New York City approved five ballot proposals that were backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, according to The Associated Press. The measures could help his efforts to build housing and expand outdoor dining and bike lanes. Opponents had argued that they would limit public input on projects.

Faces are getting longer at Ken Paxton’s watch party in Dallas. One man, upset about early votes in favor of Paxton’s Democratic rival for Senate, James Talarico, walked by the press and said loudly, “This is how countries go into revolution.”

Senator Darline Graham, the Republican who was defeated in a stunning upset in South Carolina, just took the stage at her watch party in Columbia, S.C. She said she had just gotten off the phone with Dr. Annie Andrews, her Democratic opponent, and congratulated her on becoming the first female senator elected in the state.“It is clear that we as conservatives have work to do, and that work starts tonight,” she said.

In Ohio, Sherrod Brown currently leads Senator Jon Husted by less than two percentage points. But the majority of the votes left to be tallied are in areas that have typically been more favorable to Democrats. The largest share of votes left are coming from Franklin County, home of Columbus, where Brown is currently leading by more than 30 percentage points.
Our election forecast considers a Brown victory very likely.
Democrats have now flipped six House seats held by Republicans, three of them in the critical presidential battleground state of Pennsylvania.

In South Carolina, Annie Andrews promises to be “an independent voice who will work with everyone” in the Senate. Without mentioning her defeated Republican opponent, she alludes to Darline Graham’s appointment and how it did not sit well with many voters. “Nobody in Washington recruited me to run,” Andrews said. “Nobody handed me a seat in the United States Senate. And nobody wrote me a script. I owe no one in Washington anything.”

Hundreds of supporters have been partying for hours waiting to celebrate Dr. Annie Andrews’s victory in the South Carolina Senate race. They greeted her to shouts of “Annie!” when she finally took the stage. “You have shown the nation what is possible,” she told them, noting she would be the first pediatrician in the Senate, and the first woman elected to the chamber from the state. (The interim Republican senator, Darline Graham, was appointed to the role.)

Across the country, counties that have a majority of white working-class voters, a key component of President Trump’s base, have swung toward Democrats.

The group, which has overwhelmingly supported Republicans over the last decade, swung about 15 percentage points toward Democrats. In Iowa’s Dubuque County, where Trump won by nine percentage points in 2024, Josh Turek is ahead by five points. In our

Representative Rob Bresnahan Jr., a Pennsylvania Republican who emerged as one of the most active stock traders in Congress, was defeated by Paige Cognetti, the Democratic challenger, according to The Associated Press.

Cognetti, the mayor of Scranton, made Bresnahan’s stock trading a centerpiece of her pitch to voters, hammering him for profiting from trades while in office despite running on a pledge to ban the practice.

Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania. The left is likely to point to his victory as another sign that populist policies can appeal in swing districts.

Thomas DiNapoli, a Democrat, is set to become the longest-serving comptroller in New York State history, defeating a Republican businessman, Joseph Hernandez, according to The Associated Press. DiNapoli, who has held the office for 20 years, faced his first competitive primary in June and defeated two challengers from the left.
He prides himself on being free of scandal. “Unlike every other position in the state government,” DiNapoli told The New York Times this spring, “I haven’t had to resign.”

In downtown Atlanta, Senator Raphael Warnock of Georgia congratulated Senator Jon Ossoff, “his brother from another mother,” as Warnock put it. “Jon Ossoff and I are ready to get into some more good trouble on behalf of the people of Georgia,” Warnock said in an homage to the late congressman and civil rights activist John Lewis, a mentor to both senators. Then Warnock turned to the victory of Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms, another Democrat.

“I had to facetime my 10-year-old daughter and tell her that for the first time ever in the history of our republic, we have a Black woman who is a governor,” Warnock said. “That’s good news for all of our little girls, and indeed for all of our children, because every child ought to have a path.”

An election-night watch party for the South Carolina Republican Party in Columbia, S.C., started out upbeat, with guests posing for pictures and saying that they expected Senator Darline Graham to pull through her close Senate race. But the mood curdled as it became clear that Dr. Annie Andrews, Graham’s Democratic opponent, would deliver a stunning upset in the deep-red state.

Guests turned their chairs away from tables full of pork sliders to face billboard-sized TV screens that were full of disappointing news for their party. Some called Ubers. Leeds Barroll, 74, a lawyer who donated to Graham’s campaign, said he was surprised that the race was not closer. “I thought she would have been a great senator,” he said of Graham. Several attendees repeated the same word over and over: “Wow.”

Bob Brooks, a Democratic retired firefighter and union leader who spoke candidly during his campaign of relying on public housing and food stamps after his family’s home burned down, flipped a House seat in Pennsylvania’s Lehigh Valley, according to The Associated Press, handing Democrats a crucial victory in a competitive district.

He unseated Representative Ryan Mackenzie, a Republican who flipped the Seventh Congressional District two years ago. Brooks focused his campaign on Mackenzie’s support of President Trump’s agenda, which Brooks argued had driven up costs. His victory appeared to vindicate Democrats’ efforts to appeal to working-class voters; Brooks will be among the few House Democrats who did not graduate from college.

A number of Maine’s 400-plus localities have finished counting their votes, and Susan Collins is improving on President Trump’s margin in 2024 in many of them — a sharp departure from Republican fortunes elsewhere tonight. Collins, though, is in a unique position as the only Republican incumbent running in a state the president lost in the last three elections. To keep her seat, she will need to perform well across most of the state.

“This is a mandate to deliver big change,” Representative Greg Casar, a Texas Democrat who leads the Congressional Progressive Caucus, said in a statement as returns continued to roll in showing favorable results for Democrats. “Tonight is the beginning of the end of the Trump era. Tomorrow we begin building the better world that comes next.”

The election of Keisha Lance Bottoms, a Democrat, as Georgia governor could have some impact on the 2028 presidential race. Some Democrats are hoping that Senator Jon Ossoff, another Georgia Democrat who won tonight, or Senator Raphael Warnock will make bids for the White House in 2028.

If Ossoff were to become president, Democrats could rest easy that the party would keep the vacated Senate seat, at least for a while — because a Governor Bottoms would appoint a temporary successor until a special election could be held. Warnock’s term ends on Jan. 3, 2029, less than three weeks before the scheduled swearing-in of the 48th president.

Representative Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic minority leader from New York, celebrated with his staff in Washington while watching election results roll in as more candidates in his party won House seats.

The loss by Darline Graham is, among other things, a black eye for the data-center industry, which made a late play to try to help her with the first spending of its kind. The data-center industry set up a new super PAC this fall and the group
chose Graham as its first candidate to back
. The politics of data centers are going to remain dicey going forward.

Democrats are making significant inroads into Republican territory in their battle for control of the House, flipping Republican-held seats in northern New Jersey, western North Carolina and in the Lexington area of Kentucky.

And the night is still early, with other G.O.P. districts appearing in jeopardy. Democrats seem to be finding opportunities to expand the electoral map beyond their most obvious pickup targets, raising the stakes for Republicans as more competitive races are decided.

content.text: In South Carolina, Annie Andrews is projected to win a state that President Trump carried by nearly 18 percentage points in 2024. Voters there expressed deep concerns about Darline Graham’s experience in a recent
Times/Siena
poll in the state.

The poll found that half of likely voters, including 18 percent of Republicans, said that they did not think Graham had the “right experience to be an effective senator.” In contrast, 54 percent of voters, including 22 percent of Republicans, said that Andrews did.

Florida voters approved a ballot measure that would cut property taxes on primary residences, according to The Associated Press. The tax cut, promoted by Gov. Ron DeSantis, a Republican, is expected to cost local governments billions of dollars in revenue, potentially forcing them to scale back services.

Senator Darline Graham’s projected loss is an astonishing rebuke of President Trump by voters in South Carolina. After former Senator Lindsey Graham died, Trump quickly endorsed his sister during the Republican primary to replace him, a move that many conservatives in the state viewed as bypassing the will of South Carolina voters.
Trump held three rallies in the state to try to lift Graham’s candidacy. But though he handily won South Carolina in his presidential runs, he could not help Graham across the finish line.

Annie Andrews will be the first woman elected to represent South Carolina in the Senate. It’s a slight distinction from Senator Darline Graham, the first woman appointed to represent the state in the chamber after the death of her brother, Senator Lindsey Graham.

Annie Andrews, a Democrat, has defeated Senator Darline Graham, a Republican, in South Carolina, according to our projections. It’s the second Republican-held Senate seat that the Democrats have won tonight, putting them two away from the four seats they would need to retake the chamber.

The fact that Trump proceeded with the war in Iran, which he never made an active case for with the American public, will be where most of the focus is. But the seeds of this evening began early on in his second term, including with some in the White House not realizing that the Jeffrey Epstein files were an issue that the president’s base cared about, as opposed to just an online area of intrigue.
And an early warning sign was the anger that some previously supportive podcast hosts showed toward the president. Chief among them was Joe Rogan, who condemned the president’s immigration crackdown.

Maryland voters approved an amendment to their state constitution to allow mid-decade congressional redistricting. The move is expected to result in a new congressional map for 2028 in which Democrats who control the state legislature are likely to eliminate the state’s lone Republican-held House seat.
Another upset might be brewing in Mississippi, where Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, a Republican,
holds only a narrow lead

over Scott Colom, a Democrat, with about half of the vote counted. The race is now considered a tossup, according to our estimates, with a disproportionate number of votes left to be counted from the Mississippi Delta, the state’s most heavily Black and Democratic region.

A tranche of ballots that election officials in Westchester County, N.Y., were unable to process because of difficulties with the ballot-scanning machines will be counted tomorrow starting at 11 a.m. and will continue until they are finished, according to a consent order that a State Supreme Court justice just signed. Lawyers for the State Democratic and State Republican Party, endorsed the plan, and the ballots will be counted under supervision of lawyers from both sides.
This
counting delay may end up affecting

how soon a result is known in one of the most competitive House races in the country, which is taking place outside New York City. Representative Mike Lawler, the incumbent Republican, is facing Cait Conley, a Democrat.

Rebecca Bennett, a Democrat in New Jersey, has become the first Democrat to unseat a Republican incumbent this year, defeating Representative Tom Kean Jr. She is among a cohort of military veterans whom Democrats have recruited and supported in 2026. “Female veterans and women with national security backgrounds are uniquely positioned at being able to flip seats red to blue,”
she told me last year

Michigan has its first completed county, Luce, a small rural area in the state’s Upper Peninsula. The county has shifted around five percentage points toward Dr. Abdul El-Sayed compared with the 2024 presidential election, a smaller shift than in many other competitive states tonight. But President Trump won Michigan by under two percentage points, so El-Sayed does not require as drastic of a shift to win.

The state’s biggest counties were some of the first to report, and the remaining votes, which are largely from rural counties, are expected to be favorable to Pete Ricketts, the Republican incumbent.

Still, Osborn is doing slightly better than he did in his ultimately unsuccessful 2024 campaign against Deb Fischer. At this point in the night in 2024, Osborn led by a little over nine percentage points; this year, he’s ahead by more than 13.

content.text: There are so many questions right now about what comes next, across Washington and across the Republican Party. The MAGA movement will still exist. But the notion that this is a durable coalition that will outlast President Trump, as his advisers had hoped, has suffered some blows tonight.

Sherrod Brown has run for Senate in Ohio three times in the last eight years. Between his 2018 and 2024 re-election campaigns, eight counties that had voted Democratic flipped to Republicans, helping contribute to his defeat. This year, based on the votes reported so far, five of those counties have swung back in his favor.

In Texas, the Houston area is a key part to any statewide victory as it contains roughly a quarter of the state’s voters. In Harris County, which includes Houston, James Talarico is leading Ken Paxton by more than 30 percentage points, with about three-quarters of the expected vote in. By comparison, Kamala Harris carried the county by only six percentage points in 2024, and Beto O’Rourke carried it by about 17 points in 2018.

Talarico is also seeing shifts his way in Montgomery County, which is just north of Harris and is historically a Republican stronghold. President Trump carried that county by 45 percentage points in 2024. With about 70 percent of the expected vote having been reported, Paxton leads Talarico by a more modest 21 points.

The Tennessee governor’s race remains surprisingly close between Senator Marsha Blackburn, a Republican, and Jerri Green, a Memphis councilwoman and the Democratic nominee. David Hatley, a conservative-leaning independent, has siphoned away more than 100,000 votes, making it a closer-than-expected contest so far.

The Democrats are on track to win the national House popular vote by 12 percentage points, according to our estimates. That would be the largest popular victory in the national congressional vote for either party since 1982 — back when Democrats ran up the score nationwide with overwhelming support in the South.

James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Texas, is heading toward victory, according to our estimates, with a greater than 95 percent chance to win. A Democratic victory of any size is extraordinary in Texas, which has symbolized the Republican Party’s hold on the heartland for a generation, but Talarico is on track for a jaw-dropping margin given the state’s conservative tilt.

Stefany Shaheen, a Democrat, won the First Congressional District in New Hampshire, defeating Anthony DiLorenzo, a Trump-endorsed businessman. The district is a classic House battleground that has flip-flopped between Republican and Democratic control five times since 2002.
At the Democratic watch party in Manchester, Shaheen was joined by her family onstage, including her mother, the retiring Senator Jeanne Shaheen.

Adam Hamilton, the Democrat, won the county by double digits after President Trump won it by 40 percentage points just two years ago. The shift is one of many in majority-Hispanic areas around the country tonight.
